Someone is selling you a course that will “make you rich.” You ask: what result, if it doesn’t happen in three months, would tell me it doesn’t work? If the answer is always “You just didn’t apply it right,” the claim can’t be tested.

You’re convinced late-night phone use is why your kid’s grades dropped. You set the test: if we turn the phone off at 10 p.m. for a month and nothing improves, I’m wrong and I’ll look for another cause.

detect: When you’re extremely sure about something, or someone offers you a claim that no possible result could ever prove wrong. And in any argument that’s going around in circles.
respond: Ask yourself or the other person: “What would I have to see to say I’m wrong?” Write it down before you start looking. If there’s no answer, the view needs a second look, or it isn’t the kind of view that can be debated at all.

notConfuse.name: Bayesian Updating
notConfuse.diff: The falsifiability test is something you ask before the evidence comes in, to set up the test. Updating is what you do after the evidence arrives: you shift your confidence to match it.

limits: Not everything that matters in life can be tested this way, like values and tastes. Also, one piece of evidence against your view doesn’t have to knock the whole thing down; the measurement itself might be off. The question exposes stubbornness, but it doesn’t settle everything on its own.
sources: Popper, K. (1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Hutchinson.
Popper, K. (1963). Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge. Routledge & Kegan Paul.

name: Premortem
oneLine: Before you start a plan, imagine it has already failed, and ask: “Why did it fail?”

examples.text: Before your sister’s wedding: “Imagine the wedding was a mess. Why?” One person says the venue opened late; another says the photographer has no backup if they cancel. Now you can fix those things ahead of time.

Before launching an ad campaign: “It’s a month from now and the campaign flopped. What happened?” Someone says we targeted the wrong audience; someone else says the budget ran out in a week. Now you have a real list of risks.

Driving to the beach for the weekend: “Imagine the trip was a disaster.” A flat tire, no gas station on a long stretch of highway, the Airbnb canceled. So you check the tires and confirm the booking the day before.

detect: Before any plan involving money, time, or lots of people. Especially when everyone is excited and nobody wants to be “the one who rains on the parade.”
respond: Sit down with the group (or by yourself) and say: “It’s six months from now, and the plan failed badly.” Everyone spends a few minutes writing reasons on their own. Read them out, then pick the top three to deal with now.

notConfuse.name: Hindsight Bias
notConfuse.diff: Hindsight bias is feeling, after something happens, that it was predictable all along. A premortem uses the same “looking back” move, but before you begin, so you still have time to fix things.

limits: Taken too far, it can turn into pessimism that stalls everything. And it only reveals the risks you can imagine; some things no one will see coming, however hard they think. The goal is to improve the plan, not cancel it.
sources: Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review, 85(9), 18–19.
Mitchell, D. J., Russo, J. E., & Pennington, N. (1989). Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2(1), 25–38.

name: Appeal to Consequences
oneLine: Judging an idea true or false because its outcome would be good or bad, not because of the evidence.

examples.text: “If the test shows something, it’d be a disaster, so there’s definitely nothing wrong.” And so they never get the test done.
“If that crypto platform turns out to be a scam, I’ve lost my life savings. So there’s no way it’s a scam.”
“If that catch gets overturned, we’re out of the playoffs. So it was obviously a catch.”

detect: Separate two questions: “Is this true or not?” and “Do I like what follows from it?” If your answer to the first comes from the second, you’re looking at an appeal to consequences.
respond: “I get that the outcome would be hard, but that’s not evidence it isn’t true. Let’s find out first, and then figure out how to deal with it.”

notConfuse.name: Appeal to Emotion
notConfuse.diff: An appeal to emotion stirs up your feelings so you’ll agree. An appeal to consequences is narrower: it judges whether an idea is true by its outcome. Thinking about consequences is fine when deciding what to do; the mistake is letting them decide what’s true.

sources: Bennett, B. (2017). Logically Fallacious: The Ultimate Collection of Over 300 Logical Fallacies (Academic ed.). eBookIt.com.

name: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
oneLine: Painting the target after you shoot: grabbing a slice of data that happens to show a pattern, ignoring the rest, and saying “See? Not a coincidence.”

examples.text: After the season ends, a fan digs through the team’s results until he finds they won every game played on a Thursday, and posts: “Thursday is our day. Not a coincidence.” He had no prediction about Thursdays before he went looking.
“Three people on our street have the same illness. It must be the cell tower on that roof.” Nobody checked whether that number is actually unusual for how many people live there.
A video: “The numbers in your birthday hold a secret!” It collects every number that matches and stays quiet about every one that doesn’t.

detect: Ask: was this pattern defined before we looked at the data, or picked out afterward? And where’s the rest of the data that didn’t make it into the story?
respond: “Let’s set the prediction first, then test it on new data. If the pattern is real, it’ll show up again.”

notConfuse.name: Cherry Picking
notConfuse.diff: With cherry picking, you already have a view and you select what supports it. With the Texas sharpshooter, there was no view at the start: you find a cluster by chance, then build a story around it.

sources: Bennett, B. (2017). Logically Fallacious: The Ultimate Collection of Over 300 Logical Fallacies (Academic ed.). eBookIt.com.

name: Nirvana Fallacy
oneLine: Rejecting a good solution because it isn’t perfect, by comparing it to an ideal solution that doesn’t exist.

examples.text: “Seatbelts don’t save everyone in a crash, so what’s the point?”
“The new system still has bugs, so let’s go back to paper.” And paper has way more problems.
“If I can’t save $500 a month, I’m not going to save at all.”

detect: When you hear “But that won’t solve the whole problem,” ask: compared to what? Is this solution better than what we have now or not?
respond: “Right, it’s not perfect. But the question isn’t whether it’s perfect. The question is whether it’s better than what we’ve got.”

notConfuse.name: False Dilemma
notConfuse.diff: A false dilemma hides the options in the middle. The nirvana fallacy rejects all the real options because it measures them against one that doesn’t exist.

sources: Demsetz, H. (1969). Information and efficiency: Another viewpoint. Journal of Law and Economics, 12(1), 1–22.
Bennett, B. (2017). Logically Fallacious: The Ultimate Collection of Over 300 Logical Fallacies (Academic ed.). eBookIt.com.

name: Endowment Effect
oneLine: We value something more just because it’s ours, so we ask more for it than we’d ever pay to buy it.

examples.text: “My car is worth $18,000.” Every listing and trade-in offer says about $14,500, but you’re sure they “just don’t get it.”
You list your used phone on Facebook Marketplace and get annoyed when someone haggles. Yet you haggle on every used phone you buy.
Your closet is full of clothes you haven’t worn in years, but every time you go to donate them, they feel “still perfectly good.”

detect: Ask: if this weren’t mine and I saw it for sale, what would I pay? If that number is way below what I’m asking, that’s the endowment effect.
respond: Look at what similar items actually sold for, not just asking prices. And have someone with no attachment to it estimate the price for you.

notConfuse.name: Loss Aversion
notConfuse.diff: Loss aversion is the general feeling that losses hurt more. The endowment effect is one of its results: giving up something you own feels like a loss, so you inflate its price.

evidence: Strong, but debated: some experiments found it shrinks or disappears when the procedure changes
sources: Thaler, R. (1980). Toward a positive theory of consumer choice. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 1(1), 39–60.
Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. H. (1990). Experimental tests of the endowment effect and the Coase theorem. Journal of Political Economy, 98(6), 1325–1348.

Plott, C. R., & Zeiler, K. (2005). The willingness to pay–willingness to accept gap, the "endowment effect," subject misconceptions, and experimental procedures for eliciting valuations. American Economic Review, 95(3), 530–545.

name: IKEA Effect
oneLine: We see something as better and more valuable when we put effort into making it ourselves, even if it’s ordinary or worse than the store-bought version.

examples.text: You cooked a new recipe for the first time, it came out just okay, and you can’t figure out why the family isn’t as excited as you are.
You spent three days shooting and editing a video, and you don’t get why it’s doing worse than one you threw together in 15 minutes.
You defend the idea you sweated over with everything you’ve got in the meeting, even when a coworker’s idea is simpler and better.

detect: Ask: if someone else had made the exact same thing, would it look this good to me?
respond: Get feedback from someone who didn’t see the effort behind it. And at work, if you can, evaluate ideas without the owners’ names attached.

notConfuse.name: Endowment Effect
notConfuse.diff: The endowment effect happens with anything you own, even a gift. The IKEA effect needs effort: the more work you put into something, the more it’s worth in your eyes.

evidence: Moderate — the finding has replicated, but there are still relatively few studies
sources: Norton, M. I., Mochon, D., & Ariely, D. (2012). The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 22(3), 453–460.

name: Mere-Exposure Effect
oneLine: We like something more just because we’ve seen or heard it a lot, even without paying attention to it.

examples.text: A commercial jingle you never really noticed is suddenly stuck in your head a month later, and at the store your hand goes straight to that brand.
A creator you didn’t know or care about shows up in your feed twenty times, and now you watch their videos to the end.
A new coworker you weren’t sure about, and after two months of sitting next to them you actually like them, without anything special happening.

detect: Ask: do I like this because it has a real advantage, or just because I’m used to seeing it?
respond: When choosing between two options, write down the pros of each on paper. And remember: an ad that runs over and over isn’t convincing you, it’s getting you used to it.

notConfuse.name: Illusory Truth Effect
notConfuse.diff: The mere-exposure effect is about liking: we warm up to what’s familiar. The illusory truth effect is about believing: a statement we hear a lot feels more true. They’re from the same family.

evidence: Strong, replicated in many studies — though too much repetition can flip it into boredom
sources: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt. 2), 1–27.
Bornstein, R. F. (1989). Exposure and affect: Overview and meta-analysis of research, 1968–1987. Psychological Bulletin, 106(2), 265–289.

name: Peak–End Rule
oneLine: We remember an experience by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by the whole thing or how long it lasted.

examples.text: The day at the beach was crowded and hot the whole time, but it ended with ice cream on the boardwalk, so on the drive home everyone says, “What a great day.”
A customer waited on hold for half an hour, but the rep solved the problem kindly at the end, so they gave the service five stars.
The team looked awful for eight innings, then hit a walk-off home run, and everyone leaves the stadium saying, “What a game.”

detect: Ask: am I judging the whole experience, or just its strongest moment and its ending? Try to remember the ordinary stretch in the middle.
respond: Before deciding whether to repeat an experience or avoid it, remember it from start to finish. And if you provide a service, care about the ending, but don’t let it cover up a problem in the middle.

notConfuse.name: Availability Heuristic
notConfuse.diff: The availability heuristic is judging how often something happens by how easily it comes to mind. The peak–end rule is about memory of a single experience: we sum it up in two moments.

evidence: Moderate — replicated in many experiments, but it doesn’t always outweigh how long the experience lasted
sources: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405.
Redelmeier, D. A., & Kahneman, D. (1996). Patients' memories of painful medical treatments: Real-time and retrospective evaluations of two minimally invasive procedures. Pain, 66(1), 3–8.

name: Curse of Knowledge
oneLine: Once you know something well, it’s hard to imagine someone else not knowing it, so you explain it as if they already do.

examples.text: The teacher says “This part is obvious” and skips three steps in the problem, and the whole class is lost.
You send a client an email full of phrases like “Q3 roadmap,” “KPIs,” and “circling back on the deck,” and they have no idea what you want from them.
You’re showing your dad something on his phone: “Tap here, then here,” way too fast, and you get frustrated that he isn’t following.

detect: Ask: if I didn’t know this yet, would I understand what I just said? If there’s a word an ordinary person wouldn’t know, the curse of knowledge is probably at work.
respond: Explain it to someone outside the topic and ask them to say it back in their own words. And use an everyday example instead of the technical term.

notConfuse.name: False Consensus Effect
notConfuse.diff: The false consensus effect is thinking people think and choose like you. The curse of knowledge is thinking they know what you know. The first is about opinions; the second is about information.

evidence: Moderate — the finding has replicated, but its size depends on the kind of information and the situation
sources: Camerer, C., Loewenstein, G., & Weber, M. (1989). The curse of knowledge in economic settings: An experimental analysis. Journal of Political Economy, 97(5), 1232–1254.
Newton, E. L. (1990). The rocky road from actions to intentions (Doctoral dissertation). Stanford University.

name: Illusion of Control
oneLine: We think we can influence things that are actually up to chance or outside our control.

examples.text: “I’ll pick my own lottery numbers instead of a Quick Pick. That way my odds are better.” The drawing is random either way.
You sit in the same spot on the couch and wear the same jersey every game so your team will win.
You press the elevator button five times in a row, as if that will make it come faster.

detect: Ask: if I didn’t do this at all, would the outcome actually be different? Do I have evidence, or is it just a feeling?
respond: Separate what’s in your hands from what isn’t, and put your time and money into the first. If your rituals make you happy, keep them, just don’t bet money on them.

notConfuse.name: Gambler's Fallacy
notConfuse.diff: The gambler’s fallacy is thinking chance is “due” and will even out. The illusion of control is thinking you’re the one steering the chance.

evidence: Moderate — the effect exists, but its size varies a lot with the situation
sources: Langer, E. J. (1975). The illusion of control. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(2), 311–328.

name: Just-World Belief
oneLine: We want to believe people get what they deserve, so when something bad happens to someone, we tend to look for a mistake they made that explains it.

examples.text: Someone gets their phone snatched on the subway, and instead of helping, people say: “Well, why did you have it out in a crowd?”
A coworker is let go in a round of layoffs, and you hear: “They must have been slacking on something.” Even though the cut hit the whole department.
A post about someone who got scammed, and the top comments are: “Serves them right for being greedy.” Before anyone even asks how the scam worked.

detect: If you catch yourself asking “What did they do to deserve this?” before “How can I help?”, pause. And ask: could this have happened to anyone in their place?
respond: Start with empathy and help. Questions about causes can come later, framed as “How do we prevent this?” not “Who do we blame?” And if someone is blaming the victim, calmly say: “This could happen to any of us.”

notConfuse.name: Fundamental Attribution Error
notConfuse.diff: The attribution error is explaining people’s actions by their character and ignoring circumstances. The just-world belief has a different motive: we need to feel the world is orderly, and that what happened to someone else won’t happen to us.

evidence: Moderate — the idea has support from many experiments, but the ways it’s measured have been criticized
sources: Lerner, M. J., & Simmons, C. H. (1966). Observer's reaction to the "innocent victim": Compassion or rejection? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 203–210.
Lerner, M. J. (1980). The Belief in a Just World: A Fundamental Delusion. Plenum Press.

name: False Consensus Effect
oneLine: We think most people think and choose like we do, more than they actually do.

examples.text: You made an ad that fits your own taste and figured “Everyone will love it like I do.” Then the engagement came in weak.
“Who even eats this without hot sauce? Everybody likes it spicy.” And you’re the only one in the house who does.
“I love working late, so I’m sure the whole team is fine with a 9 p.m. call.” Nobody was asked.

detect: Ask: do I have numbers showing people are like me, or is it just my feeling? And the people I talk to, are they like everyone, or like me?
respond: Ask people who are different from you before you decide. At work, run a quick poll or test with a small sample before assuming.

notConfuse.name: Bandwagon Effect
notConfuse.diff: The bandwagon effect is changing your view to go along with the crowd. The false consensus effect is the reverse: assuming the crowd is already with you.

sources: Ross, L., Greene, D., & House, P. (1977). The "false consensus effect": An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 13(3), 279–301.
